edible_parts: Grain, fresh or dried; immature ears; pollen; the smut fungus (huitlacoche).
other_uses: Domesticated from Balsas teosinte in south-western Mexico roughly 9,000 years ago and now the most-grown grain on earth. The tall sister of the Three Sisters: it gives the beans something to climb while the squash shades their roots. Stalks and husks are used for fodder, thatch, cordage and tamale wrappers. Native range: the Balsas River valley of south-western Mexico, where it was domesticated. Now grown on every continent except Antarctica.
prep: Sweet corn is eaten raw or briefly cooked. Flint, flour and dent corns are dried and ground — and for anything but sweet corn, nixtamalisation (cooking the grain in wood ash or lime, then hulling it) is not optional: it is what makes the niacin available and prevents pellagra.
harvest: Sweet corn at the milk stage; dry corn once the husks brown and the kernels dent.
soil: Rich, deep, well-drained soil; a heavy nitrogen feeder.
risks: A maize-dominated diet without nixtamalisation causes pellagra (niacin deficiency). Corn is wind-pollinated and crosses freely — plant in blocks, not rows, and keep distance between varieties you want to keep true.
sources: World Checklist of Vascular Plants (WCVP) — distribution
